note: One entry per clip. 'segments' is the narration: one line per on-screen caption, in the order the captions appear in the scene.

segments.caption: Diffusion models learn to generate by learning to undo noise.
segments.text: Diffusion models learn to generate by learning to undo noise. We start from a real backbone, x zero, drawn here as sixteen C alpha points in a short helix, which is illustrative. Training runs in two directions.

segments.caption: One forward step adds a little Gaussian noise to every point.
segments.text: The forward direction adds a little Gaussian noise at every step. Each point drifts by a random amount, and after the first few steps the helix is still obvious.

segments.caption: After t steps the result is one weighted mix of structure and noise.
segments.text: You never have to take the steps one at a time. After t steps, x t is a single weighted mix: the square root of the signal weight times x zero, plus the square root of one minus that weight, times one Gaussian draw.

segments.caption: The schedule sets those weights: at t = 500 the structure is nearly gone.
segments.text: The schedule fixes those weights. With beta rising from zero point zero zero zero one to zero point zero two over a thousand steps, the signal weight is zero point nine five at step one hundred, zero point seven two at two hundred fifty, and zero point two eight at five hundred.

segments.caption: By the last step nothing of the original structure is left.
segments.text: By step nine hundred ninety-nine the signal weight is zero point zero zero six: a Gaussian cloud. Every protein ends in the same place, which is exactly why sampling can start from noise alone.

segments.caption: Noising needs no learning, so training pairs are free.
segments.text: Noising needs no learning at all, just a random number generator. The network only ever learns the way back. One real structure gives a thousand training examples, one for every step.

segments.caption: The network sees a noisy structure and the step number, and predicts the noise.
segments.text: A single network sees the noisy structure x t and the step number t, and predicts the noise that was added. Predicting the noise and predicting the clean structure are the same job: either one gives you the other.

segments.caption: One reverse step moves a little toward that prediction, then adds fresh noise.
segments.text: One reverse step moves a little way toward the predicted clean structure, then adds a little fresh noise. Repeat from a thousand down to one. The fresh noise is what keeps the samples diverse.

segments.caption: Run the step a thousand times and noise becomes a plausible backbone.
segments.text: Run that step a thousand times and the Gaussian cloud tightens into a backbone that could fold. The drawing is illustrative, but the trajectory is real: structure appears gradually, not all at once.

segments.caption: New starting noise gives a new structure every time: generation, not retrieval.
segments.text: Start from different noise and you get a different structure. This is generation, not retrieval: none of these has to appear anywhere in the training set.

segments.caption: RFdiffusion builds its denoiser out of a structure predictor.
segments.text: R F diffusion, from Watson and colleagues, fine-tunes the structure predictor Rosetta Fold into its denoiser. It works on residue frames, a C alpha position plus an orientation, predicts the clean structure at every step and feeds it back as a template, and runs about two hundred steps. One twist: for motif scaffolding, adding no fresh noise on the way back worked better in seventeen of the twenty-three solved problems.

segments.caption: A backbone is a shape, not a protein: ProteinMPNN writes the sequence.
segments.text: R F diffusion makes a shape, not a protein. Protein M P N N then designs sequences for that backbone, typically about eight of them. Those sequences are what you can actually order, express, and test.

segments.caption: AlphaFold 3 has a diffusion module too, straight on the atoms.
segments.text: Alpha Fold three, from Abramson and colleagues, uses a diffusion module as well, but it predicts raw atom coordinates directly, with no amino acid frames and no torsion angles. Dropping that protein-specific machinery is what lets one model cover proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, and ions.

segments.caption: Unconditional sampling makes some protein, not the one you need.
segments.text: Unconditional sampling gives you a valid structure, but not the one you need. The samples and the numbers in this clip are illustrative. A real design project asks for something specific: hold this functional motif in place, or bind this target protein.

segments.caption: Conditioning pins part of the structure and lets the rest form around it.
segments.text: Conditioning is the direct answer. Give the denoiser the motif's coordinates and hold them fixed at every step. The motif never moves, and the scaffold is sampled, so one motif gives you many different scaffolds.

segments.caption: Guidance is a different lever, from image diffusion, not used by RFdiffusion.
segments.text: Guidance is a different lever, borrowed from image diffusion. Mix the conditional and unconditional predictions: zero point two, plus three times zero point five minus zero point two, gives one point one. A larger w follows the condition harder and cuts diversity. R F diffusion does not do this; it conditions the denoiser directly.

segments.caption: On 25 motif-scaffolding benchmarks, RFdiffusion solved 23.
segments.text: Watson and colleagues report that on twenty-five motif-scaffolding benchmarks, R F diffusion solved twenty-three, against nineteen for R F joint inpainting and fifteen for hallucination, using one set of settings for every problem. Note that this success is scored in silico.

segments.caption: Binders against five targets: 19% worked in the lab.
segments.text: Designed binders were tested against five targets, among them influenza hemagglutinin and P D L one. Nineteen percent worked experimentally, from fewer than a hundred designs per target. The best flu binder reached twenty-eight nanomolar, and a cryo E M map matched the design to zero point six three angstroms.

segments.caption: The in silico judge can share the designer's blind spots.
segments.text: Read the in silico numbers with care. The designs are scored by Alpha Fold family predictors, from Abramson and colleagues, trained on the same structures, so the designer and the judge can agree and both be wrong. The nineteen percent is the number that counts, because it came from a wet lab.
